content: Taste buds are small, specialized structures located on the upper surface of the tongue, the soft palate, and the epiglottis. They are responsible for detecting and transmitting information about the taste of food being consumed. The human tongue contains approximately 10,000 taste buds. The majority of taste buds on the tongue are situated on raised protrusions of the tongue's surface called papillae. There are four distinct types of papillae: 1. Fungiform papillae: These papillae are slightly mushroom-shaped when viewed in cross-section. They are predominantly located at the tip (apex) of the tongue and along its sides. They are innervated by the facial nerve. 2. Filiform papillae: These are thin, elongated, V-shaped conical structures that do not contain taste buds. They are the most numerous type of papillae and serve a mechanical function rather than a gustatory one. They are characterized by increased keratinization. 3. Foliate papillae: These papillae appear as ridges and grooves located on the lateral margins of the posterior part of the tongue. The anterior foliate papillae are innervated by the facial nerve, while the posterior foliate papillae are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve. 4. Circumvallate papillae: These are relatively few in number, typically ranging from 3 to 14 in most individuals. They are located at the back of the oral part of the tongue, arranged in a circular row just anterior to the sulcus terminalis. These papillae are associated with the ducts of Von Ebner's glands and are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve. There are five recognized taste sensations: Sweet, bitter, and umami (sometimes referred to as savory) are mediated by G-protein-coupled receptors. Salty and sour tastes are detected via ion channels. Contrary to the popular misconception that different areas of the tongue are responsible for specific taste sensations, all taste qualities can be detected across the entire tongue. This misunderstanding originated from a mistranslation by Harvard psychologist Edwin G. Boring of a German paper written in 1901. Taste sensitivity is distributed throughout the tongue and extends to other regions of the mouth where taste buds are present, such as the epiglottis and soft palate. Each taste bud is flask-shaped, with a broad base resting on the connective tissue (corium) and a narrow neck that opens to the surface through a small orifice called the gustatory pore. Taste buds are composed of two main types of cells: 1. Supporting (sustentacular) cells: These cells are primarily arranged like the staves of a barrel, forming an outer envelope for the taste bud. Some supporting cells are also located within the interior of the bud, interspersed among the gustatory cells. 2. Gustatory (taste) cells: These are chemoreceptor cells that occupy the central portion of the taste bud. They are spindle-shaped and contain a large, spherical nucleus near the center of the cell. The peripheral end of each gustatory cell extends to the gustatory pore as a fine, hair-like filament called the gustatory hair. The central process of the cell extends toward the deeper end of the bud, terminating in single or bifurcated varicosities. Nerve fibers, after losing their myelin sheaths, enter the taste bud and terminate in fine extremities between the gustatory cells. Other nerve fibers branch between the supporting cells and also terminate in fine extremities. These latter fibers are believed to be associated with general sensation rather than taste perception.
